paragraphs: Americans into a Number of Small Private Circles

One might suppose that the final consequence and necessary effect of democratic institutions is to throw all members of the community together in private as well as public life, and to force them all to live in common. But that would be to give the equality that arises from democracy a very crude and oppressive form. No state of society and no laws can make men so alike that education, fortune, and tastes will not put some differences between them. And although different men may sometimes find it in their interest to combine for the same purposes, they will never make it their pleasure. They will therefore always tend to evade the provisions of the law, whatever those may be. Departing in some one respect from the circle within which they were meant to be confined, they will set up, close beside the great political community, small private circles united by the similarity of their conditions, habits, and manners.

In the United States the citizens have no kind of superiority over one another; they owe each other neither obedience nor respect. They all meet to administer justice, to govern the State, and in general to treat the affairs that concern their common welfare. But I have never heard that anyone has tried to bring them all to follow the same amusements, or to enjoy themselves indiscriminately in the same places of recreation. The Americans, who mix so readily in their political assemblies and courts of justice, make a habit on the contrary of dividing carefully into small, distinct circles, so as to enjoy the pleasures of private life by themselves. Each of them is willing to acknowledge all his fellow citizens as his equals, but he will receive only a very small number of them as friends or guests. This seems to me quite natural. As the circle of public society widens, one can expect the sphere of private intercourse to narrow. Far from supposing that the members of modern society will end up living in common, I fear they may end by forming nothing but small coteries.

Among aristocratic nations the different classes are like vast chambers: one cannot get out of them or enter them. The classes have no communication with one another, but within each one’s bounds men necessarily live in daily contact. Even if they would not naturally suit, the general conformity of a similar condition brings them closer together. But when neither law nor custom claims to establish frequent and habitual relations between certain men, their dealings arise from a chance likeness of opinions and tastes, and so private society is infinitely varied. In democracies, where the members of the community never differ much from each other and naturally stand so close together that they could at any moment be merged into one general mass, numerous artificial and arbitrary distinctions spring up. Through them each man hopes to keep himself apart, for fear of being carried off in the crowd against his will. This can never fail to happen, for human institutions may be changed, but man cannot. However much a community may try to make its members equal and alike, the personal pride of individuals will always seek to rise above the line and to create somewhere an inequality to their own advantage.

In aristocracies men are separated from one another by lofty, fixed barriers; in democracies they are divided by a multitude of small, almost invisible threads, which are constantly broken or moved from place to place. Thus, whatever the progress of equality, a great number of small private communities will always form within the general bounds of political society in democratic nations. But none of them will resemble in its manners the highest class in aristocracies.
